blocks.text: A prominent nucleus is present in all eukaryotic cells (at centre in animal cells while pushed to side in plant cells). The spherical nucleus typically occupies about 10 percent of a eukaryotic cell's volume. It serves as information processing and administrative centre of the cell. It performs two major functions: it stores the cell's hereditary material (DNA) and coordinates the cell's activities e.g., growth, protein synthesis and cell division.

blocks.alt: A nucleus cut open: the nuclear envelope with nuclear pores surrounds threads of chromatin and a dark central nucleolus. Sheets of endoplasmic reticulum studded with ribosomes wrap round one side and are continuous with the outer membrane of the envelope.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.11: The structure of nucleus (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.11).

blocks.text: The semifluid matrix found inside the nucleus is called nucleoplasm. Within the nucleoplasm, most of the nuclear material consists of chromatin that organizes to form chromosomes during cell division. The nucleus also contains one or more nucleoli, which synthesize ribosomes.

Building blocks of DNA and RNA and ATPs are allowed to enter into the nucleus. Ribosomal subunits which are built in nucleoli are the examples of materials that are allowed to leave the nucleus and enter the cytoplasm.
The Nuclear Envelope and Nuclear Pores

The nuclear envelope is a double-layered membrane that encloses the contents of the nucleus during most of the cell's lifecycle. The space between the double layers is called the perinuclear space and is connected with the rough endoplasmic reticulum. During cell division, the nuclear envelope disintegrates, but reforms in the daughter cells. On the inner side of nuclear envelope, there is a protein lining, called nuclear lamina. It binds to chromatin to give it structural support.

blocks.alt: The nuclear envelope drawn as a slab: the outer nuclear membrane on top with a ring of ring subunits around a pore, and at the front the outer membrane, the space between the membranes, the inner nuclear membrane and the nuclear lamina. At the front left a cut pore complex shows ring, column, annular and lumenal subunits and the nuclear basket below.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.12: The structure of nuclear envelope and nuclear pore complex (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.12).
blocks.long_description: The nuclear envelope drawn as a slab. Its top face is the outer nuclear membrane, with a ring of ring subunits around a pore; at the front edge the layers show the outer membrane, the space between the membranes, the inner nuclear membrane and the nuclear lamina below it. At the front left a pore complex is cut through: ring subunits on top, column subunits forming the walls, annular subunits across the centre, lumenal subunits in the space between the membranes, and fibrils forming the nuclear basket hanging into the nucleus.

blocks.text: The nuclear envelope has tiny holes known as nuclear pores. These pores regulate the passage of molecules between nucleus and cytoplasm. Nuclear pores are permeable to small molecules. Some larger proteins, e.g., histones, are also allowed to enter into nucleus. A nuclear pore is made of an elaborate structure called the nuclear pore complex. It is composed of several subunits. These are; annular subunit (surrounding the inside of the pore), column subunit (making the wall of the complex), ring subunit (attached to the outer side of the column subunit), and lumenal subunit (anchoring the pore complex into the nuclear envelope). Tiny fibrils usually extend form the complex and make a basket-like structure on the nuclear side of the complex.

In cells that produce large amounts of protein, and thus require significant numbers of ribosomes, the size of the nucleolus is considerable.
At the onset of mitosis, the single nucleolus present in cell disappears, and after division new nucleolus is formed from the NORs.

The nucleolus is a prominent darkly stained structure in the nucleoplasm. There may be one or two nucleoli in a nucleus. Nucleoli manufacture the subunits that combine to form ribosomes. Nucleoli are formed at certain sites in chromosome, called Nucleolus Organizer Regions (NORs). The DNA found at NORs encodes the ribosomal RNA (rRNA).

The nucleolus consists of granular and fibrillar components, and DNA. The granules consist of ribosomal subunits that have already been formed. The fibrils are composed of the raw materials of ribosome subunits i.e., rRNA molecules and associated proteins.

blocks.alt: A nucleus bounded by the nuclear envelope with pores; in its centre lies the dense, dark nucleolus, and chromatin threads radiate from it through the nucleoplasm.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.13: The nucleolus within a nucleus (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.13).

blocks.text: Nucleus contains string-like fibres, collectively called chromatin. It is composed of DNA and proteins. The structure of chromatin reveals that it is made of a series of bead-like structures, called nucleosomes. In a nucleosome, DNA strand wraps around groups of small proteins called histones.
Inside the nucleus of every human cell, there is a 6 feet long DNA. It is subdivided into 46 individual molecules (each 1.5 inches long), one for each chromosome.

During interphase (when the cell is carrying out its normal functions), the chromatin is dispersed throughout the nucleus in the form of a tangle of fibres. When the cell begins to divide, all chromatin strands are compressed into specialized structures, the chromosomes. A chromosome is made of arms, called chromatids, and a central point, called centromere.

There are two types of chromatin. Euchromatin is the genetically active chromatin involved in transcribing RNA to produce proteins. The other kind of chromatin is termed heterochromatin. Its DNA is genetically inactive.

blocks.alt: Stages of packing DNA: chromatin inside the nucleus near a nuclear pore; a thick chromatin fibre formed by a coil of nucleosomes; nucleosomes, each with DNA wound round a core of histones, joined by linker DNA; the DNA double helix. Beside them, a condensed chromosome of two chromatids joined at the centromere, with its arms and telomeres at the ends.
blocks.caption: Figure 3.14: Condensation of chromatin to form a chromosome (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 3.14).

blocks.text: The number of chromosomes within the nuclei of an organism's cells is species-specific. Human diploid cells (those that are not gametes) have 46 chromosomes. The chromosome number may be as low as 2, as in some ants and roundworms, or more may be than a thousand, as in the Indian fern (Ophioglossum reticulatum), which has 1,260 chromosomes. It means that the number of chromosomes in a species does not correlate to the complexity of the organism.
